routes.title: The Downtown Loop
routes.blurb: Roughly 1.7 miles, mostly flat with one climb back up from the lake. Budget 90–120 minutes at a casual pace, more if you linger at the waterfront.

steps.directions: Face south and start walking down Church Street Marketplace.
Continue south to the bottom of Church Street, where City Hall faces the park.
Head west one block on College Street to the library.
Backtrack toward Church Street and head north on Cherry Street toward Battery Park. The route goes slightly uphill, then down toward the bluff.
Walk south along Battery Street, back the way you came, taking in the historic houses.
Continue south and then down the hill toward the waterfront — via Pine Street or the Battery Street stairs/path — to Union Station.
Walk north along the waterfront bike path toward the old power plant.
Walk back south along the waterfront path, past Union Station, toward ECHO.
Walk out onto the bike path or the fishing pier just south of ECHO for the breakwater view.
Head back up College Street toward downtown, retracing part of your earlier route. This stretch is uphill.
Walk half a block to Nectar's.
Walk northwest back up to Church Street and climb to the top.

pins.title: The Unitarian Church
pins.tease: The white steeple everyone gives directions from, and the Revere bell it used to hold.
pins.stand_at: Stand on Church Street at the Pearl Street crossing, facing the white church across the street.
pins.script:
Look straight up the street. That white spire at the end of Church Street is the thing everything down here aims at. Two heavy brick buildings frame it: the Masonic Temple, finished in 1898, and the Richardson Building, 1895, put up to hold Burlington's largest department store. The state's own historic district file says the church provides a focal point for the area, and that directions in Burlington are frequently given in relation to it.

The building went up in 1816. The congregation had bought the land two years before that. Five acres of overgrown pasture on the northern edge of the village, for $1,000. The meeting house cost $22,185.34. The timbers came from the Browns River Valley. The brick was fired in Burlington. The nails were hammered by hand.

The architect was Peter Banner, working out of Boston. There is evidence that Charles Bulfinch supervised or amended Banner's plan. The tower rises about 170 feet, though the spire you are looking at is a 1958 replica. Lightning took the original in 1954.

Here is the part most people walk past. The first bell in that tower was cast by Paul Revere's foundry in October 1816. It weighed about thirteen hundred pounds. Then somebody rang it too hard. In 1828 it cracked and had to be recast. In 1928 it was replaced outright with a bell from the Meneely foundry.

The church was dedicated on January 9, 1817. Its congregation calls it the oldest surviving place of worship in the city.

You are standing at the top of the street. Everything else on this walk sits downhill from here. The marketplace. The park. The library. The bluff over the lake. In 1974 these three buildings around you were listed together on the National Register as the Head of Church Street Historic District.

pins.title: Church Street Marketplace
pins.tease: A Copenhagen street a student saw in 1962, rebuilt here
pins.stand_at: Stand mid-block on Church Street between Bank and Cherry, facing downhill toward City Hall.
pins.script:
Brick under your feet, no cars, benches down the middle. Behind you at the top of the slope, the white church spire. Ahead of you, downhill, City Hall.

Until 1980 this was a street. Traffic, curbs, parked cars, the whole thing.

The idea of closing it goes back to 1958, to a round of urban renewal discussions. It got its champion in 1962, when a Burlington architecture student named Bill Truex went to Copenhagen and saw the Stroget, a street the Marketplace's own history describes as a traffic-snarled nightmare that had been handed back to people on foot.

Burlington tested the idea before committing to it. A one-day street fair in 1971 drew about 15,000 people. A week-long fair the next year drew an estimated 50,000. That was the proof.

On July 7, 1980, the two blocks between College and Cherry closed to traffic for good. More than a year of construction followed, on a $6 million design by Carr, Lynch Associates with C.E. Maguire supervising the engineering, paid for with a federal grant and a city bond that Burlington voters passed. The Marketplace opened on September 15, 1981.

Now the part that surprises people who assume it arrived all at once. It didn't. On opening day, only two blocks of it existed. The top block, Cherry up to Pearl, the one you walked down to get here, was not closed and resurfaced in brick until 1994. And the block in front of City Hall, Main to College, was not finished until 2005.

So the four-block street with roughly 86 storefronts that everyone treats as one thing took 25 years to become one. It is listed on the National Register of Historic Places, and the American Planning Association named it one of America's Great Public Spaces. The stretch you would swear was always here, the block facing City Hall, has only been free of cars since 2005.

pins.title: City Hall Park
pins.tease: This lawn was voted into existence before the streets were drawn
pins.stand_at: Stand by the fountain in the middle of City Hall Park, facing the brick and marble front of City Hall.
pins.script:
Fountain in front of you. A ring of trees. And on the far side, brick and carved marble with a clock tower on top: City Hall.

This lawn is older than almost everything around it, and it was decided in a house three blocks downhill. In June 1798 the proprietors of Burlington held their last series of meetings at Gideon King Junior's house on King Street. At one of them, William Coit presented a final plan for the city, the grid that downtown streets still run on. And at those same meetings the proprietors voted to set aside the land you are standing on.

For its first hundred years or so this was Court House Square. It sits partway between the waterfront and the commercial cluster up on College Hill, which may have been a compromise between two sets of business interests that each wanted the center of town nearer to them.

City Hall came much later. Burlington's 1850s city hall was badly built and falling apart. The replacement went to McKim, Mead and White of New York, with William M. Kendall as architect, and it opened to the public on May 12, 1928. It cost $475,000, which came in $25,000 under budget.

Look at what it is made of. The red brick, the carved marble, the granite, the slate on the roof. Nearly every finish material in that building was produced in Vermont. That was the point of it.

In 1983 the park and the buildings around it were listed on the National Register as the City Hall Park Historic District, eight acres bounded by Church, College, Main and St. Paul. Most of those buildings went up between about 1880 and 1930, replacing wooden ones.

The park itself had been reserved 185 years before that listing, by men who had not yet finished drawing the streets.

In addition they voted to set aside the land now known as City Hall Park.'

pins.title: Fletcher Free Library
pins.tease: A gift, a steel baron, and a ravine that nearly ate it
pins.stand_at: Stand on the College Street sidewalk in front of the library's stone steps, facing the columns.
pins.script:
Columns, stone steps, a Beaux-Arts front sitting right on College Street. This is the Fletcher Free Library, and Burlington has had a free library for more than 150 years.

It started with a gift. On July 14, 1873, Mrs. Mary L. Fletcher and her daughter, Miss Mary M. Fletcher, gave the city of Burlington $20,000 to found it. Half was to be spent on books. The other half started an endowment.

The library lived inside the old city hall building and outgrew it by 1901. That same year Andrew Carnegie gave $50,000 for a new building. A Burlington architect, Walter R. B. Willcox, won the competition to design it. It was dedicated and opened for business on August 17, 1904, the first of the four Carnegie libraries in Vermont.

Now the problem nobody planned for. There was a ravine on this site, and the ravine had been filled in. In 1973 the northwest corner of the foundation settled and the building took structural damage. The books had to leave. First to Contois Auditorium, then to the basement of Memorial Auditorium. Demolition was on the table.

What saved it was a committee with a very plain name: the Committee to Save the Fletcher Free Library Building. They got the building onto the National Register of Historic Places in August 1976. A federal Economic Development Administration grant of $234,000 paid for stabilization and exterior repairs in 1977.

Then Burlington voters approved a $2.4 million bond for an addition, and that addition was dedicated on January 4, 1981. It is the modern wing behind the old stone one, and it is the reason this is still a working library and not a plaque.

Exterior preservation work on the 1904 Carnegie building ran from 2024 into 2026, paid for through Save America's Treasures and Vermont historic preservation grants.

pins.title: Little Italy
pins.tease: The ground you are standing on is what the bulldozers made
pins.stand_at: Stand at the foot of Cherry Street on the Battery Park Extension, by the green state historic marker, facing east up Cherry Street.
pins.script:
You are on a strip of grass at the foot of Cherry Street. The lake is below you to the west. The street climbs away from you to the east. There is a green state historic marker here. Read it if you want. Then look up Cherry Street, because that is where the neighborhood was.

Roughly six blocks, running east from Battery and Pearl to Pine Street, south to College, and back west to Battery. Houses, gardens, shops, families. The households were Italian American, and also French Canadian, Syrian, and other backgrounds. The interpretive signage puts it carefully. Many of the people, but not all the people, were the sons and daughters of Italian immigrants.

On May 17, 1966, a bulldozer crushed the walls of a tenement building on Cherry Street, then moved to the next building and did the same. Over the following two years, more than 160 buildings came down, housing 157 families, 67 individuals and 41 businesses. Twenty-seven acres cleared. It was called the Champlain Street Urban Renewal Project.

The last person out was Victoria Dutra, of 12 Cherry Street. Her home was demolished in 1968.

Here is the part that is easy to miss while you are standing on it. This ground is part of the project too. In 1966 the city acquired the buildings on the west side of Battery Street and took them down so that Battery Park could be extended south. The reason given at the time was to open up more of a lake view from the renewal area.

So the view you have right now was produced by the same clearance that removed the neighborhood behind you.

In 2011 the Vermont Division for Historic Preservation designated the former urban renewal neighborhood as Little Italy. The marker beside you was dedicated on October 8, 2011, forty-three years after the last house came down.

pins.title: Battery Park
pins.tease: Cannon on this bluff, then a glass furnace just north of it, then a park.
pins.stand_at: Stand at the western rim of Battery Park, at the railing above the bluff, facing the lake.
pins.script:
You are on the edge of a bluff. The lake is in front of you, the Adirondacks across it, and the ground drops away hard from your feet. That drop is why this is Battery Park.

During the War of 1812 the United States military put cannon up here to protect the harbor and stationed roughly 4,000 soldiers on and around this ground. Burlington sat within reach of the Canadian border, and the lake was the road an invasion would use. The park takes its name from the artillery, not from anything that happened afterward.

What you see now is a few green acres on the bluff. A bandshell, a playground, monuments. A bronze of the Civil War general William W. Wells. A red oak carving of Chief Grey Lock by the sculptor Peter Wolf Toth.

And here is the stretch of this place's history that almost nobody tells you.

Within about fifteen years of the soldiers leaving, the ground just north of here was heavy industry. In 1827 Doctor John Peck and Professor James Dean established the Champlain Glass Company on the former battery campsite. It is described as the first extensive manufacturing concern in the town. It covered about two acres. It employed about 100 people. It made window glass.

Frederick Smith, who arrived in Burlington the same year the works opened, ran the glassworks from 1834 until 1850, when the cost of fuel made it unprofitable and it shut down. Smith then subdivided the property himself and laid Park and Front Streets across the site.

So the order on this ground is artillery, then a glass furnace on the blocks to the north, then a park. And the glass was not a small footnote to the neighborhood. It was the neighborhood. An 1839 survey labels the neighborhood north of the battery Glassville.

pins.title: Battery Street
pins.tease: The old waterline, and the shipyard that launched the world's second steamboat
pins.stand_at: Stand on the west sidewalk of Battery Street at College Street, facing the lake where the ground drops away.
pins.script:
Battery Street, with the ground falling away in front of you toward the rail line and the lake. Hold onto that drop, because it used to be the edge of the water.

This street was called Water Street. The lakeshore came right up to it. The shoreline is now hundreds of feet further out than it was. Everything between you and the water down there is made land, filled in across the 1800s for wharves, lumber yards and railroad track.

A block south of you the state's historic survey marks out the Battery Street Historic District, and describes it as Burlington's earliest settlement, an area of mixed commercial, light industrial and residential use developed from 1790 onward. It is on the National Register.

The man who ran the lake from here was Gideon King Junior. Between 1790 and 1812 he controlled lake traffic, working a route between Burlington, Saint Johns in Quebec, and Whitehall, New York. His house still stands at 35 King Street, a few blocks south of you, and the survey calls it one of Burlington's oldest structures.

And at the foot of King Street was Burlington's only shipyard. What came out of it was the steamboat Vermont, which the state survey calls the world's second commercial steamboat. John and James Winans built her here, and when they went to launch her in 1809 the engine was so heavy the hull stuck fast in the mud. They had to get her up onto logs and roll her into the lake.

Down at the foot of Maple Street, the old South Wharf, known as the Salt Dock, went in in 1810 to get cargo off the boats.

One more thing happened on this street. The second story of the Pomeroy House was a classroom for University of Vermont medical students from 1804 to 1822. The first regular lectures on anatomy and surgery ever given in Burlington were delivered in that house, to twelve students, in the winter of 1814.

pins.title: Union Station
pins.tease: The man who drew Grand Central drew this too
pins.stand_at: Stand on the walkway at the foot of Main Street, just east of the station, facing the clock in the stone above the entrance.
pins.script:
Look up at the clock set into the stone above the entrance. Around it, carved scrolls and swags of fruit and flowers tied with ribbons. And on top of the whole composition, an hourglass with wings.

This is Burlington Union Station. It opened in January 1916, and it was the city's second union station. In 1867 the Vermont Central Railroad built a permanent station on fill at the foot of College Street. Four years later that railroad leased the Rutland Railroad, and the depot became a union station. Union means more than one railroad, sharing one building.

For the replacement, the city donated land and 15,000 dollars to build a new depot and reroute the tracks. The Central Vermont and the Rutland, who would jointly own it, put up the remaining 150,000 for a steel-framed neoclassical building in buff brick with cream limestone trim.

Here is the part people miss. The architect was Alfred Fellheimer. He had been involved with the design of Grand Central Terminal in Manhattan, and he already had extensive experience with railroad structures. The man who helped shape the biggest station in America also drew this one, at the bottom of Main Street.

Then the trains stopped. The Central Vermont ended passenger service in 1938. The Rutland ran passenger trains here until 1953, when a strike ended them. Two years after that, Green Mountain Power converted the station into office space. The building stayed. The trains did not. Main Street Landing owns it now, and it holds businesses and organizations.

Walk around to the lake side and you will find a platform and a canopy. The Vermont Agency of Transportation built them, with site preparation done in 2020 and 2021.

On July 29, 2022, Amtrak began direct service to Burlington when the Ethan Allen Express was extended north from Rutland.

Sixty-nine years separated the last Rutland passenger train from the first Amtrak train to pull in behind this building.

pins.title: The FRAME
pins.tease: They fixed the power plant by taking most of it away
pins.stand_at: Stand on the path just east of the red steel structure, facing it with the lake behind it.
pins.script:
In front of you is a red steel skeleton with the sky showing through it. No roof. Almost no walls. That is not decay. That is the design.

This was the Moran plant, Burlington's own municipal generating station. Ground was broken in 1952. It came online two years later and was fully finished in 1955, a thirty megawatt coal fired power plant right here on the waterfront.

In 1977 it did something unusual. The plant made its first experimental conversion from coal to wood chips. A second unit followed two years after that. Vermont trees, chipped and hauled in, turned into electricity on the shore of Lake Champlain.

The plant was decommissioned in 1986. Then it sat. For more than three decades a brick shell occupied some of the most valuable open ground in the city, and nobody could agree what it should become. On March 4, 2008, Burlington voters approved a 21 million dollar renovation plan for it. That plan was never built.

Here is the surprise. The idea that finally worked was to take most of the building away.

In August 2020 the city broke ground. Crews peeled back the brick exterior, kept the steel superstructure underneath, and left it standing open to the weather. Not restored. Not replaced. Reduced to its bones, and then painted a striking red.

The ribbon was cut on November 15, 2022, on about six and a half million dollars of work. It ran over because they found PCBs in the ground during demolition. Doreen Kraft, who runs Burlington City Arts, said that day marked the transitioning of this space from the unsustainable energy of coal to the cleanest, most renewable energy that there is: creativity.

Look into the northwest bay. Two custom swinging benches hang there, designed and manufactured with Generator, a Burlington maker space. The group that raised money for them pulled in over 22,000 dollars in five weeks of crowdfunding, matched with 40,000 from the state's Better Places program.

With that six and a half million they added free public wifi, seasonal restrooms, and a community idea board, inside the rib cage of a coal plant.

pins.title: ECHO
pins.tease: Eighty-four million gallons of fuel used to sit here
pins.stand_at: Stand at the foot of College Street where the pavement meets the waterfront, facing west toward the lake, with ECHO on your left.
pins.script:
On your left is ECHO, the lake aquarium and science center at the foot of College Street. Beyond it, open water. Now put fuel tanks on this ground.

By 1958, by UVM's count of the waterfront, there were eighty three fuel tanks holding a total of eighty four million gallons. This was not a park. It was a tank farm with rail yards, and the railroad held the filled land it stood on.

By 1975 the city had an ordinance on the books giving the oil companies twenty years to vacate the property. In 1986 the bike path along the water was completed with state and federal money. But the decisive fight happened in court.

In 1989 the Vermont Supreme Court ruled, in State versus Central Vermont Railway, that the filled land here was impressed by the public trust doctrine. And the court held that only the Legislature could decide what public trust land is for. So the Legislature made a list. Parks and open space. Recreation. Marinas open to the public on a nondiscriminatory basis. Water dependent uses, boating and related services. And in 1991 it added arts, educational and cultural uses, including museums.

Here is the surprise. The waterfront around you is largely not natural shoreline. It is fill, dumped to make room for the railroad. And it was that artificial origin, land made out of a public lake, that gave the city its legal opening.

Since the 1960s the city has acquired more than sixty acres of this waterfront. That 1991 list is what made this building legal.

ECHO itself was dedicated on May 31, 2003. The name stands for ecology, culture, history, and opportunities. It grew out of the Lake Champlain Science Center, which opened here in 1995 in borrowed Naval Reserve space, and it carries the name of Senator Patrick Leahy, who secured the federal funding for it.

Inside are about fifty species of live animals: fish, reptiles, amphibians.

ECHO says the building that went up on this reclaimed ground was Vermont's first LEED certified green building.

pins.title: The Breakwater
pins.tease: In 1876 this wall of stone caught five people out of a gale
pins.stand_at: Stand at the railing on the outer pier deck west of the Burlington Community Boathouse, facing straight out at the low stone line offshore.
pins.script:
Look straight out at the water. That long low line of stone running parallel to the shore is the Burlington Breakwater. It is not a reef. It is a nineteenth-century engineering project, and it is still doing the job it was built for.

Work began in 1836. The first section was V shaped and about a thousand feet long, finished in 1854. The engineers estimated it at 28,727 dollars. By 1844 they had spent eighty thousand. Between 1867 and 1874 they added 831 feet at the north end and 617 feet at the south, bringing it to 2,517 feet. A final 364 foot section was finished in 1890, set off from the rest by a two hundred foot gap.

Underneath the waterline it is timber. Log cribs, joined by notched corners, laid on a rubble foundation and packed with rubblestone. Hemlock in the lower levels, white pine in the upper. Most of the upper cribbing has rotted and been replaced with stone since, and the lake facing side was armored with riprap in the early 1960s. It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on June 6, 2003, as a significant example of nineteenth century timber cribbed breakwater construction.

Wooden lighthouses were first placed on the ends in 1857. The northern tower burned in 1870. The southern light was knocked over in a storm in 1876.

That same year, this wall of stone saved five lives.

On December 9, 1876, a powerful winter gale caught the sailing canal boat General Butler as she came up the lake. Her steering mechanism broke. Her captain, William Montgomery of Isle La Motte, rigged a tiller bar to the steering post and tried to work around the breakwater. He did not make it. The Butler crashed headlong into the stone, and one by one every person aboard jumped onto the breakwater as she went down.

Then they were stranded on a rock wall in a December gale. A Burlington ship chandler named James Wakefield and his son rowed out in a 14-foot lighthouse boat and took all five to safety.

The General Butler is still out there. She rests in 40 feet of water, about 75 yards west of the southern end of the breakwater, a Vermont underwater historic preserve.

pins.title: Memorial Auditorium
pins.tease: This building exists because voters refused a smaller one
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Main Street sidewalk below the auditorium, near the corner of South Union Street, facing the front steps.
pins.script:
The big building above you on this corner has been locked since 2016. Memorial Auditorium. Look at the scale of it. This was built to hold thousands of people at once.

It exists because Burlington citizens refused something smaller.

In 1925 the editor-in-chief of the Burlington Free Press called for a large, separate memorial auditorium with tablets on the walls of the main lobby, rather than a smaller memorial hall folded into the new city hall then being planned for Church Street. In January 1926 the mayor's office presented city hall plans with a 1,000-seat auditorium inside. Many citizens complained. They wanted a separate building, somewhere else, and bigger.

The city gave way. In February 1926 a new city hall design appeared without an auditorium, by the firm of McKim, Mead and White. That is the building on Church Street. And a separate memorial auditorium, to hold more than three thousand, was announced for this corner, to go to the voters.

In March 1926 they approved it. The architect was Frank L. Austin of Burlington, who also designed the Central Fire Station and the junior high school. Ground was broken about six weeks later.

Then the money ran out. Twice. Work stalled through most of 1926, until that December voters authorized another thirty thousand dollars. By April 1927 they approved another 100,000 dollar bond. The original plan had been that the auditorium would cost no more than 150,000 dollars, funded from the remaining balance of a 750,000 dollar bond. In January 1927 the paper put the total, with heating, lighting and all fixtures, at 233,185 dollars. By April the contract came in at 204,629 dollars.

It opened on March 28, 1928, to a crowd of three thousand. The Burlington Symphony Orchestra played the first concert here that April, to seventeen hundred people. The 1929 Burlington Automobile Show was advertised as the largest show north of Boston. Simon and Garfunkel played this room on October 13, 1968. Three songs from that night ended up on a box set.

It went on the National Register on October 13, 1988. Not on its own, but as a contributing building in the Main Street and College Street Historic District. It was closed in December 2016 on the recommendation of the City Engineer.

pins.title: Nectar's
pins.tease: A Greek immigrant let an unknown band flail here for two years
pins.stand_at: Stand on the north sidewalk of Main Street outside 188 Main Street, facing the storefront and its sign.
pins.script:
You are outside 188 Main Street. A brick building with a marquee that went dark in May 2025. For fifty years this was Nectar's.

Nectar Rorris came to the United States from Greece in 1956. He borrowed money from family, the way he said everyone did, and in 1975 he opened a restaurant and bar here. It sold gravy fries. French fries under turkey gravy. Fifty years later, at the end, people were still shouting for them.

In the mid 1980s a young Burlington band got a residency in this room that ran close to two years. They were still working out what they were. Rorris let them do it in public, night after night, in front of people eating gravy fries.

The band was Phish.

Here is the surprise. Rorris never expected any of it. The wire story put it this way: he never imagined the club he opened would become synonymous with a jam band, and he credited Phish with the national spotlight. His own words were shorter. Phish made Nectar's. The same story said Phish credited him right back, for giving them a stage to experiment on when they were starting out. In 1992 they named an album A Picture of Nectar, after the man and after this bar. When the place closed, the band said nothing.

Then Main Street got torn up. Construction cut the foot traffic. Costs climbed. In May 2025 Nectar's announced it would close for the summer and blamed the construction. The pause was supposed to be temporary.

On July 30, 2025, the owners said it was permanent. Lease negotiations with the building's owner, Joe Handy, had not worked out.

A former employee, counting what went with it, listed a music venue, and employment for a lot of chefs, a lot of sound engineers, a lot of bartenders, a lot of servers. He said that until the rest of Main Street is finished, he does not see a way this makes sense.

Fifty years of a Burlington bar ended over a lease, a street that was dug up, and, as one local writer put it, a thousand smaller cuts before that. Main Street was finished in July of 2026. The city threw a block party. Nectar's had been dark for thirteen months.

pins.title: St. Joseph
pins.tease: Protestant landowners donated the stone for a poor French parish
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Allen Street sidewalk across from the church, facing its main doors.
pins.script:
In front of you is the largest church building in Vermont. Saint Joseph, on Allen Street. Look at the walls. They are red sandstone, and at the base they are more than five feet thick.

The parish is older than the building. It was founded in 1850, and the diocese calls it the first French-Canadian national parish in New England. Before that, Burlington's Catholics, Irish and French Canadian together, shared one church. They shared a faith. They did not share a language, or customs, and the French often felt like second-class members of an Irish congregation.

So in 1850 they got their own. The first church was roofed and ready for Mass by Christmas that year, described at the time as a bit like the stable at Bethlehem because it had no decoration. It took seven more years to finish the plastering.

Then the parish outgrew it. In 1883 Bishop DeGoesbriand approved a larger church. He acknowledged the parish was not rich. He urged them to finish it in two years anyway.

The man who drew it was Reverend Joseph Michaud, a self-taught architect from Montreal, working in a grand classical style. The parish says the result resembles the chapel at the Palace of Versailles. The numbers are 176 feet long, 81 feet wide, 55 feet to the ceiling, seating for more than 1,200.

Here is the part that surprises people. This parish was poor. Parishioners who were carpenters, masons, plasterers and glaziers worked on it full time, or gave a day or more a week. They paid for it with picnics and dances, concerts and card parties, house-to-house collections, and annual bazaars at City Hall that ran two and three weeks.

And the red sandstone you are looking at was a gift. It came from a local quarry, and the Protestant landowners donated it to the French Catholic parish.

Work took more than four years. The first Mass in the new church was celebrated on Easter Sunday, April 10, 1887. It was named a co-cathedral in October 1999. The 1887 building cost around 85,000 dollars.

pins.title: Elmwood Cemetery
pins.tease: The northern half was segregated, and nobody toured it
pins.stand_at: Enter through the gate on Elmwood Avenue and walk a short way in, then stand among the oldest slate headstones in the southern half.
pins.script:
You are standing among slate headstones. Look at how many of them are worn blank, and how many are simply gone. Nobody has a complete list of who is buried here.

Start with a correction. This is not Burlington's first burying ground. From the town's charter in 1763 the public burial ground was two acres out on Colchester Avenue, now part of Greenmount Cemetery. That ground got crowded, and its plan was irregular, so a second cemetery was established. This one. A parish history compiled in 1983 records that it was called Elmwood, that it had been used from 1794, and that it was not laid out in an organized plan until 1813.

So for its first twenty years, this was a burying ground with no map.

The names people used to come here for are the North End notables. Frances Allen, known as Fanny, who was Ethan Allen's widow. John Norton Pomeroy. The early families whose surnames are on Burlington street signs.

Now turn toward the northern half.

That half was segregated when the cemetery was built. Burlington's Black residents were buried there. Among them are Revolutionary War veterans, and people who provided safe harbor to others seeking their freedom on the Underground Railroad. Some worked as servants and laborers. Others were skilled barbers, cooks, nurses and homemakers. The historian Elise Guyette has been pulling those lives back out of the record, and Preservation Burlington now runs a tour of that half of the ground.

Burials here effectively stopped around 1869, during a cholera epidemic in the city.

Which leaves the stones. Many of the markers can no longer be read at all, and Preservation Burlington is still working through them, trying to match what is left to names.

pins.title: North Street
pins.tease: A nineties survey counted twelve streetlight poles from 1925, all on one side
pins.stand_at: Stand on the northwest corner of North Street and North Winooski Avenue, looking west down North Street.
pins.script:
You are on the northwest corner of North Street and North Winooski Avenue. Look west, down North Street. Now look at the streetlight poles. When this district was surveyed in the nineteen nineties, about twelve of the originals still stood, put up around 1925, steel standards of the type made for thoroughfares. Their lanterns were gone and they carried modern heads. Every survivor was on the north side of the street.

This street is a National Register historic district, seventy-two contributing buildings, and it was listed for a specific reason. It is where Burlington's immigrant communities met each other.

They lived apart, and the census is blunt about it. In 1850 Burlington's population was 7,585. Of those, 2,249 were Irish, nearly thirty percent, and 890 were French Canadian. By 1910 the population was 20,468, and more than half of those people, 10,643, were first or second generation immigrants.

The neighborhoods were mapped street by street. By the 1890s the Irish community was centered along North Street between North Avenue and North Champlain. Further east, near Elmwood Avenue, was the French Canadian sector. Germans settled along lower North Avenue near the Goethe Lodge on Crowley Street. Lithuanian Jews settled near Hyde and Archibald Streets and built the Ohavi Zedek Synagogue there in 1885. That neighborhood got called little Jerusalem.

They shopped on the same street. Frank's Economy Store. Mazel's Department Store. Hyman Bloomberg's shoes. A pastry shop run by the Gelineau family.

The National Register nomination says it plainly. Each group came looking for work, found comfort and support in its own religion, and eventually moved out of the North End. North Street was the binding agent that held them together.

That nomination lists the sequence as French Canadian, Irish, German, Jewish, and finally Vietnamese. It was written before the rest of the list.

In the program's first twenty-five years, from 1989 to 2014, at least 6,300 people came to Vermont through federal refugee resettlement. That total included 1,705 Bosnians, most of them Muslims, and 1,437 Bhutanese, many of whom had been living in exile in Nepal, and about a thousand people fleeing violence in Burundi, Congo, Rwanda, Somalia and Sudan.

pins.title: Waterfront Park
pins.tease: Eighty-three oil tanks used to stand where you are standing
pins.stand_at: Stand on the promenade in the middle of Waterfront Park, on the lawn above the boardwalk, facing the lake.
pins.script:
You are standing on a lawn at the edge of a lake. Hold on to that, because for most of this city's history you could not have stood here, and you would not have wanted to.

In the eighteen hundreds this was the third busiest lumber port in the country. When the lumber companies needed more ground, they made it, filling the shallows out into the lake. Part of what is under your feet is manufactured land.

The Depression finished the lumber trade. By 1935 the failing yards had been replaced with fuel storage holding five and a half million gallons. And it grew. By 1958 there were eighty-three tanks on this waterfront holding eighty-four million gallons. Around them: rail sidings, junkyards, rusting equipment, a coal-burning power plant, and derelict boats rotting in the harbor.

Getting out of that took decades. In 1975 the city passed an ordinance giving the oil companies twenty years to leave. In a 1982 poll by a group called Citizens Waterfront, eighty-one percent of those asked wanted public access to the water. In December of 1985 a bond that would have put condominiums, a seven story hotel and a parking garage here won a majority, fell short of the two thirds it needed, and died.

Then the argument went to court. In 1989 the Vermont Supreme Court ruled that filled land on this lakefront is impressed by the public trust doctrine. It belongs to the public, and it can only be used for parks, recreation and things that actually need to be on the water. That decision let the city acquire more than sixty acres from the railroad. It also made the land cheap, because nobody could put condominiums on it anymore.

The community boathouse opened in 1988. This park, ten and a half acres of it, opened with its boardwalk in 1991.

The work did not stop there. In August of 2014 the city broke ground on the stretch north of here: a rebuilt bike path, environmental cleanup, power lines buried, and a public skate park. That package cost nine point one million dollars, and the ribbon was cut in November of 2015.

pins.title: The Coast Guard Station
pins.tease: This station began as four men tending lights out on the lake
pins.stand_at: Stand on the bike path at the Waterfront Park boat launch off Penny Lane, just east of the low Coast Guard building, facing the station and the open lake.
pins.script:
A low building at the edge of the water, with a dock, and boats made fast to it. This is 1 Depot Street. It is a United States Coast Guard station.

Which is a strange thing to find in Vermont. There is no ocean here.

The unit started in 1948, and it did not start in this building. It started as a seasonal light attendant station, four men, working the lake from out on the water. Their job was the lights and the buoys. Not rescue. Maintenance. Somebody had to keep the marks lit so boats did not run onto rock.

That job is still one of the jobs. The crew here keeps the buoys and the lights and the markers on Lake Champlain, and two shore lights up on Lake Memphremagog. There is an Aids to Navigation Team based at this same address.

But the lake got busier. Recreational boating grew, and search and rescue calls came with it, and the station changed shape around them. This building went up in 1993. A crew of roughly twenty five enlisted men and women works out of it. They run maritime law enforcement, search and rescue, and ice rescue, and their area of responsibility is all one hundred and twenty miles of Lake Champlain, plus Coast Guard Auxiliary coordination on Lake George.

The station averages over 200 search and rescue cases a year.

Now think about what season it is. Because this lake does something an ocean does not do. It hardens.

Every winter, thousands of people walk out onto Lake Champlain to fish. They tow shanties out there. They park on it.

So the winter operations at this station include ice rescue training. The Coast Guard trains here to pull people out of a hole in the middle of a road that is made of water.

pins.title: The Bike Path
pins.tease: Follow this pavement north and it runs out into the lake
pins.stand_at: Stand on the paved path at the north end of Waterfront Park, facing north along the shore.
pins.script:
The pavement under you is a railroad bed. The Rutland Railroad built the Island Line here in 1901 and ran it north out of Burlington, along this shore, and then straight out into open water.

To reach the Champlain Islands the railroad did not build a bridge. It built a causeway. Crews tipped granite and marble quarry rock into the lake for three and a half miles, from Colchester Point across to South Hero, and laid track on top of the rubble. It is still out there. You can walk on it.

Passenger service on the Island Line ended after an employee strike in the early nineteen fifties. The final trains ran in the fall of 1961. In 1963 the state of Vermont bought the abandoned Rutland lines. It left this one out.

The path came later, and it came from a vote. In 1981 Burlington voters approved a bike path on the old right of way by about three to one. It was fully funded by 1984, and by 1986 the waterfront stretch was complete. In 2010 the trail was inducted into the Rails-to-Trails Hall of Fame.

Here is the part people do not expect. The causeway has a hole in it. About two hundred feet of open water, called the Cut, where a swing bridge used to pivot aside to let boats through. The bridge is gone. The gap is not.

Since 1998, from late spring into fall, a ferry has crossed it. Not a car ferry. A bike ferry, run by the nonprofit Local Motion. It carries bicycles, trailers, wheelchairs and other mobility devices, and it takes anyone who bikes, walks or rolls out to it. No motor vehicles.

The whole trail runs about thirteen miles. Eight paved from Oakledge Park up to Airport Park, and five more of crushed gravel out on the causeway.

pins.title: The Champlain Thrust
pins.tease: The cliff above you was shoved here from miles away
pins.stand_at: Stand at the junction where the Thrust Fault Trail meets the Sunset Ridge Trail on top of the cliffs at Rock Point, above the stone staircase that leads down to the shoreline.
pins.script:
You are on the trail on top of the cliffs at Rock Point. Stay on the trail, away from the cliff edge. From here a stone staircase goes down to the shoreline, and the fault is down there at the water.

Look at the wall. There is a line running across it, roughly level, sharp as a pencil stroke.

Above the line the rock is pale, the color of sand. Below the line it is dark gray, shot through with white veins.

The pale rock on top is Dunham dolostone. It formed in the Cambrian, roughly 500 to 540 million years ago. The dark rock underneath is Iberville shale. It formed in the Ordovician, about 460 million years ago.

Read that again. The older rock is sitting on top of the younger rock. That is backwards. Rock is supposed to stack in order, oldest at the bottom.

This is the Champlain Thrust fault. During the Taconic Orogeny, the mountain-building collision that raised the Green Mountains, a whole slab of older seafloor rock was pushed up and west, over the top of younger rock. The line you are looking at is the surface it slid on.

Here is the number that does not fit in your head. The estimated displacement along this fault is 35 to 50 miles. The vertical throw right here at Lone Rock Point is about 8,850 feet. And the fault does not stop at this beach. It runs from Canada south to the Catskill Plateau in New York, about 199 miles.

Now get closer to the line itself. Between the two plates there is a zone of breccia, crushed rock and broken fragments, ground up as the slabs moved against each other. Slivers of limestone are caught in there too, torn off and carried along in the grinding.

Rock Point calls this one of the most visible and dramatic exposures of a thrust fault in eastern North America. Most thrust faults on this planet are buried, or they are somewhere you cannot get to.

This one is at eye level, on land the Episcopal Diocese of Vermont owns, on trails that are free and open to the public.

pins.title: The Ethan Allen Homestead
pins.tease: The city forgot this was Ethan Allen's house, then argued about it
pins.stand_at: Stand in the yard at the Ethan Allen Homestead, facing the small clapboard farmhouse on the rise above the Winooski River.
pins.script:
A small clapboard farmhouse on a rise. Below it, flat ground running to the Winooski River. That flat ground is the Intervale, and it floods.

Ethan Allen came here in 1787, near the end of his life, to be a farmer. He wrote to a friend that November: I have lately arrived at my new farm of 14 hundred acres, in which are three hundred and fifty acres of choice river intervale and rich upland meadow.

The house was already standing. A housewright named Josiah Averill had been hired to build it in 1785. Allen, his wife Fanny, and the rest of the household spent about three months down at Burlington Bay, staying with John Collins, while the place was finished.

Allen lived in this house for a little over a year. He died here on February 12, 1789. His hired man, Newport, gave an account of it. They had gone across the river and were coming home, and when they reached the water Allen was taken with a fit and struggled for some time.

Then the house disappeared.

Not physically. It just stopped being his. It became the Van Ness farm. The barns burned in 1914. In 1942 the Pease Grain Company renovated it, and by the 1970s it looked like every other wartime colonial revival house in greater Burlington. Nobody was pointing at it.

In 1975 the Vermont historian Ralph Nading Hill announced he had found Ethan Allen's home. He raised the money, he led the restoration, and he died just months before the museum opened in 1987.

Here is the honest part. In 2003 two preservation specialists went back through the frame, the nails and the joinery for Vermont History. Their conclusion was that the physical evidence fits a house built in 1785, and that Ralph Nading Hill probably got it right on very thin evidence.

But they also found this. The grand house Ethan had specified in a letter was never built. Ira had promised him five hundred dollars worth of building materials. Years later Fanny testified in court that the materials were never delivered.

pins.title: 88 King Street
pins.tease: The city lent its workers' pension money to house people
pins.stand_at: Stand on the north sidewalk of King Street outside the Champlain Housing Trust office at number 88.
pins.script:
You are outside 88 King Street. The building behind you is the headquarters of the Champlain Housing Trust. It went up as part of a block-wide redevelopment with twenty apartments alongside it, built to be LEED certified, and in 2009 that block won a Smart Growth award.

The organization inside is older than the building, and it began as an argument about what public money should buy.

Bernie Sanders became mayor of Burlington in 1981, the same year Ronald Reagan took office. Federal housing money was being withdrawn. Mortgage rates were in double digits. Working-class neighborhoods were under pressure from rising prices, and the city's recent record on poor neighborhoods was bulldozing them in the name of urban renewal.

A Progressive alderman named Terry Bouricius found the community land trust model. The idea is simple and strange. A nonprofit holds the land permanently. It sells only the house standing on it, at a price a working household can pay, with a resale formula that keeps the next price low too. The help stays with the home instead of leaving with the first owner.

The city's development office sent three staff to the first national gathering of land trusts, in Voluntown, Connecticut. Then it hired a technical adviser to bring the idea to Burlington's residents and find out whether it took.

It took. The Burlington Community Land Trust was incorporated in 1984, after thousands of hours of volunteer work. Among the incorporators was Howard Dean, the state's future governor.

Here is what the city actually put in. A 200,000 dollar seed grant for operations. A negotiated loan pool from a local bank. And a pair of million-dollar loans out of the Burlington Employee Retirement Fund. The pension money of city workers.

The Burlington Community Land Trust was the first municipally supported community land trust in the United States. Its first designated target area was the Old North End.

In 2006 it merged with the Lake Champlain Housing Development Corporation to become the Champlain Housing Trust. Soon after, the model won a United Nations World Habitat Award.

pins.title: Perkins Pier
pins.tease: This quiet pier was once stacked forty feet high
pins.stand_at: Stand out near the end of Perkins Pier, at the rail, facing north up the shoreline.
pins.script:
You are standing on made land. The lake used to reach further in than this. In 1810 a man named Curtis Holgate built a wharf at the bottom of Maple Street and filled part of the lake to hold it up. That is the ground under your shoes.

For a while this was the steamboat landing. Canal and stagecoach traffic was routed here by 1823, and the wharf sat at the center of one of the busiest commercial districts in town. Freight moved off boats and onto wagons right where you are standing.

Then came the wood. Look north along the shoreline and take the boats away. Fill it with lumber. Boards stacked thirty to forty feet high, covering more than thirty acres of waterfront.

By 1865 Burlington had become, by most accounts, the third largest lumber port in the country. Some accounts put it second. Only Chicago and Albany moved more. The lumber came south from Canada by boat. It got sorted and resawn here. It left by rail.

The numbers kept climbing. In 1873 this harbor handled upwards of 123 million feet of lumber in a year. At the peak, in 1889, shipments topped 375 million feet. At least twelve wharves worked the harbor.

Then it stopped. New tariffs in 1893 and 1894 cut the Canadian supply down hard. By 1926 the harbor took in about thirty boats of lumber a year.

The waterfront did not go quiet, though. It went flammable. Oil companies took over the empty wharves and built tanks on them. By 1958 there were eighty-three fuel tanks along this shore. Together they held eighty-four million gallons.

The city opened Perkins Pier the next year, in 1959.

pins.title: The Lakeside Mill
pins.tease: A cotton mill built this whole neighborhood, then sold it off
pins.stand_at: Stand on the north sidewalk of Lakeside Avenue at 128 Lakeside Avenue, looking up along the brick wall that runs the length of the block.
pins.script:
Four stories of brick. A flat roof. Windows running the length of the block. This is 128 Lakeside Avenue.

A contractor from Fall River, Massachusetts started building it on July 22, 1894. On Wednesday, January 30, 1895, the son of the mill manager started the coal-fired steam engine for the first time. Cloth started coming off the Draper looms that May.

The company did not just build a mill. It built the neighborhood. Burlington businessmen had made a deal with George Draper and Sons of Massachusetts, who made the power looms. Then the company bought the land southwest of here and filled the streets with houses. Central, Conger, Wright, Harrison. In November of 1899 the Burlington Free Press reported work moving fast on sixteen new tenement houses. Fourteen of them were doubles, six rooms a side.

A church. Grocery stores. A school. A billiard hall. It was meant to be a self-contained village, and it was the only neighborhood in Burlington a company ever built whole. The mill advertised in English and in French, and the workers came.

Then the cotton business went bad. After a long strike, production stopped for good in the spring of 1937.

Here is the part that surprises people. The company did not clear the houses out. It sold them, and it gave the workers living in them first option to buy. A duplex went for about $2,500. Families who had rented from the mill bought the walls around them, and those streets are on the National Register of Historic Places now.

The mill itself kept working. Latex, first. Then the federal government seized it in July of 1943, and Bell Aircraft leased it, and in 1944 employment here hit 2,700 people, the highest it ever was. Then General Electric bought it. Then Lockheed. Then General Dynamics, which walked out in 2010 and took 450 jobs to Williston. Just west of the mill, Blodgett finished a new oven factory in early 1946, at 50 Lakeside Avenue.

The mill building is called the Innovation Center of Vermont now.

pins.title: The Maltex Building
pins.tease: The company in this building invented Maypo
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Pine Street sidewalk in front of the four-story brick building with the tall windows.
pins.script:
Four stories of brick, tall windows, and a name across the top. Maltex. This was a cereal factory.

William J. Van Patten, a Burlington druggist and politician, founded the Malted Cereal Company in 1899 and had this building put up on Pine Street in 1900. The product was a hot cereal made from wheat and barley. It was called Maltex. The recipe outlived the factory. A company in Ohio makes it now.

Here is the part worth knowing. In the nineteen fifties the company invented Maypo, a hot oat cereal flavored with maple. This was the company that did it, and this was the building it worked out of.

The end came without warning. On May 9, 1969, the vice president of the company came in from Missouri and told the workers the factory was closing that day. Production left Vermont.

The building sat. In 1983 a man named Rick Davis bought it and cut it into space for small businesses, which is still what it is. That move, repeated up and down this street, is how a corridor of dead factories became an arts district. The South End Art Hop runs its thirty-fourth year in September of 2026, free, across more than a hundred locations along a two-mile stretch of this neighborhood.

Now stop looking at the buildings and think about the ground.

A few blocks south of here is the Pine Street Barge Canal. It is a federal Superfund site. Thirty-eight acres: a canal, a turning basin, wetlands, and a pond.

A plant on Pine Street used to make the city's gas by cooking coal. It ran until 1966. The waste went into the wetland. In the 1960s and 1970s an oil-like material began seeping out of the ground into the canal and the basin, and Burlington drinks from Lake Champlain. The Environmental Protection Agency settled on a remedy in 1998 and finished the work in 2004, capping the contaminated sediment underwater instead of digging it out.

The pond the coal tar seeped into had a name. It was called Maltex Pond.

pins.title: The Earth Clock
pins.tease: Fourteen granite stones that tell you the season by shadow
pins.stand_at: Stand inside the ring of granite stones beside the bike path at the north end of Oakledge Park.
pins.script:
Fourteen slabs of granite standing in a ring on the grass. The circle is forty three and a half feet across. The stones weigh between three and a half tons and twenty tons each.

This is the Burlington Earth Clock, and it was built in 2007 by a Vermont grassroots nonprofit called Circles for Peace. It was their first project.

It is three instruments at once. A compass, because the whole ring is aligned to the directions. A calendar, because it tracks the sun's journey north and south along the horizon through the cycle of the seasons. And a clock. There is a sundial at the center. Stand on the date line in the middle of it and your own shadow tells you the time.

Now walk south, into the park proper. About ten minutes down the path there is an oak tree with a house in it, fifteen feet up, reached by a level walkway that starts less than fifty feet from the parking lot. It is called the Forever Young Treehouse. It was finished in 2004 and built as the world's first public universally accessible community treehouse.

And past that, where the picnic shelter stands, there used to be a mansion.

Dr. William Seward Webb and his wife Lila built it in 1883 and 1884. They lived here, on a 245 acre farm with barns full of horses, Jersey cattle and sheep, before they built Shelburne Farms and moved down there. The press called it one of the handsomest places in Burlington. The family held it until 1926, then sold to Burlington investors. It became the Oakledge Manor Resort from 1929 to 1961, and then the Cliffside Country Club until 1970.

Here is how it ended. On July 19, 1971, at a quarter past nine in the morning, the Burlington Fire Department burned it down on purpose, as a training exercise. Firemen dropped a match on floors soaked with gasoline and kerosene.

In a little more than an hour the house was ashes.

pins.title: 242 Main
pins.tease: The city banned rock music, then built a punk club
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Main Street sidewalk at the west end of Memorial Auditorium, below the basement level.
pins.script:
You are at the west end of Memorial Auditorium, on the Main Street sidewalk. Look down at the basement level, under the big hall. In the southwest corner of that basement was 242 Main.

Start with a ban. In the summer of 1981, at the start of Bernie Sanders's first term as mayor, Jane Driscoll and Kathy Lawrence tried to put on a rock concert at Battery Park. They discovered the city had an ordinance prohibiting the performance of rock music on public property, enacted under the previous mayor, Gordon Paquette. They petitioned to have it lifted. Sanders agreed, temporarily. When the city's children did not turn into devil-worshipping hellions, he removed the ordinance for good, in time for a battle of the bands in this building that November.

Driscoll ran the Mayor's Youth Office, created in 1984. Teenagers kept climbing through the window of her city hall office to talk to her. She decided they needed a room of their own. Around the same time the city water department moved out of the southwest corner of this basement. It did not seem big enough for the city to use for anything else.

With a 60,000 dollar Community Development Block Grant, work began in 1985. The Vermont architect David Sellers and the designer Ed Owre helped shape the space. Some of the teenagers helped build it as part of a building class. It opened in March 1986, by Jane Sanders's account. Plenty of people in town will tell you 1985.

Here is what people forget. It was not a punk club first. It had a lunch counter staffed by teenagers slinging burgers and fries. It ran after-school programs for Edmunds Middle School kids. It was a rehearsal space for plays, a production room for a newspaper called the Queen City Special, and a set for a local-access television show. Most afternoons it smelled like hazelnut coffee and fresh-baked cookies.

Then it got loud. Operation Ivy played here. Fugazi played here in 1989. Black Flag. Converge. It was believed to be the oldest all-ages, substance-free punk club in the country, and almost certainly the only one owned and operated by a city.

The city closed the building in December 2016 for structural reasons. The last show was 21 bands.

pins.title: The UVM Green
pins.tease: Lafayette laid a stone here. It is not where he left it.
pins.stand_at: Stand on the walkway in the middle of the University Green, facing east toward the long building with the tower.
pins.script:
You are standing on a rectangle of grass that a university was built around. Look east at the long building with the tower. That is Old Mill. It is not one building.

The University of Vermont was chartered in 1791, the same year Vermont became the fourteenth state. It was the fifth college in New England, after Harvard, Yale, Dartmouth and Brown. Ira Allen led the drive to charter it and to put it here, on the hill above Burlington Bay. The bronze Ira Allen on this green is much newer. James Wilbur donated it to the university in 1921.

The first college building went up on this spot starting in eighteen oh one. On May 28, 1824, it burned to the ground. A student had been feeding wood shavings into a stove. The draft carried the glowing shavings up a brick chimney and dropped them back down onto a corner of the roof.

Burlington paid to rebuild. In August of 1824 a citizens' committee announced it had raised $8,362.

Now the part that surprises people. They did not put up one building. They put up two, three stories each, set seven or eight feet apart on purpose so a fire could not jump between them. Governor Cornelius Van Ness laid the cornerstone of North College on April 26, 1825.

Two months later Burlington got a celebrity. The Marquis de Lafayette was partway through a thirteen-month tour of all twenty-four states. On the evening of June 29, 1825, he laid the cornerstone of South College with Masonic rites, anointing it with oil, wine and corn. Then he went to dinner at Grasse Mount and left that night by steamboat.

A third building, Middle College, filled the gap in 1829. The row was finally connected in 1846.

Lafayette's cornerstone is still in that wall. It was reset there during the remodeling of 1882.

pins.title: Billings Library
pins.tease: He bought 12,000 books, then built a building around them
pins.stand_at: Stand on the grass of the University Green, back from University Place, facing east at the long red sandstone building with the deep round-arched entrance.
pins.script:
Look east across the grass. The low building of red sandstone, with the deep round arch, is Billings Library. Henry Hobson Richardson designed it. It was dedicated in 1885, and Richardson died the following year.

The building exists because of somebody else's books.

In 1882 Frederick Billings bought the personal library of George Perkins Marsh for the University of Vermont. Billings was a Vermonter, class of 1844, and by then a railroad man. Marsh was from Woodstock, and he had written the book that more or less started American conservation. His library ran to about 12,000 volumes. The university had nowhere to put them.

So Billings hired the most celebrated architect in the country to build somewhere to put them. He planned to give 75,000 dollars. Even after the ornament was cut back, the finished building cost more than 150,000 dollars.

Here is a detail to carry with you while you look at it. Richardson's design had a small turreted feature out front, and Billings did not like it. He called it a pepper-box. He wrote to the university's president suggesting that if they changed that pepper-box into a clock tower, they would get about what the two of them were thinking of. It was never done. You are looking at the version that lost the argument.

After Richardson died, his successor firm, Shepley, Rutan and Coolidge, extended the building for more stacks and added the Marsh Room on the east side.

Then the building stopped being a library. The university outgrew it and put up a bigger one in 1961. In the early 1960s Billings became the student center, and it stayed a student center for more than forty years. A snack shop in the basement of a Richardson building.

Undoing that took a renovation of about 11 million dollars, launched in June 2017 and finished the following summer.

In August 2018, one hundred and thirty-three years after it opened, this building became a library again.

pins.title: The Ethan Allen Monument
pins.tease: Vermont built the monument, then admitted it had lost the grave
pins.stand_at: Stand at the base of the tall granite column with the marble figure on top, in Greenmount Cemetery off Colchester Avenue.
pins.script:
In front of you is a column of granite with a marble man on top. One arm is up. He is demanding that the British surrender Fort Ticonderoga. This is Vermont's monument to Ethan Allen, and it stands over a question nobody has answered.

Allen went out to South Hero on February 11, 1789, to visit a cousin. On the way home he suffered a fit, and he was unconscious by the time they got him back. He died a few hours later without waking up. He was buried four days after that, here, following a large public funeral.

Then, over the next seventy years, the spot was lost.

The family reorganized the cemetery plot at some point, and the original grave marker was removed some feet from its original position. An official report in 1858 laid this out. By then Vermont was building the monument anyway.

The column went up in 1858. It is 35 feet of Doric granite on an eight-foot base with marble tablets, and the granite is believed to have been salvaged from the Vermont State House, which had burned in 1838. The fence of cast iron muskets and cannon around it dates from 1872. In 1873 an eight-foot statue of Allen in Carrara marble was set on top, carved to the design of the Boston sculptor Peter Stephenson.

Now look at the face. No portrait of Ethan Allen exists. Depictions like this one were shaped by a traditional commemorative style rather than by any attempt at accuracy. The man above you is an invention.

There is a vault under the monument. It does not hold Allen. It holds a time capsule from the time the monument was built.

Then read the inscription. Vermont chose its words carefully. It says he was born in Litchfield, Connecticut, on the tenth of January, 1737, that he died in Burlington on the twelfth of February, 1789, and that he was buried near the site of this monument.

Near.

pins.title: Hunt's
pins.tease: A song about a dairy mascot was born in this building
pins.stand_at: Stand on the south sidewalk of Main Street directly in front of the hotel entrance at 101 Main Street.
pins.script:
In front of you is 101 Main Street. Today it is a hotel. The Hilton Garden Inn, with a restaurant called the Armory Grille and Bar, and the Vermont Comedy Club at the front of the building.

From 1977 to 1988 this address was a music club. It went by the name R. W. Hunt Mill and Mining Company, which is a joke, because it was never a mill and it never mined anything. Everybody just called it Hunt's.

Before Hunt's, in the mid seventies, the room ran as the Yankee Pickin' Opry. After Hunt's closed, it became a fifties-themed nightclub called Sha-Na-Na's.

But hold on to 1985. In March of that year, a young Burlington band played this room. They came back on October 30.

That October night, they played a song here for the first time. It was called Harry Hood.

Here is where it came from. Members of that band were living at 156 King Street, a few blocks from here. Directly across from them was a Hood milk plant. At the northwestern corner of that building stood two big white tanks, and painted on the tanks was a face: Harry Hood, the mascot of the Hood dairy company.

Harry Hood was a character from a nineteen seventies television commercial. In it, people open their refrigerator and Harry Hood is standing inside. That is where the line about the lights going out comes from. It is about a refrigerator.

So a Burlington band wrote a song about the smiling man painted on the milk tanks across the street from their house, and played it for the first time in a bar on Main Street in front of whoever happened to be there on a Wednesday night in October.

That song has now been played live over 400 times.

The band was Phish. The room they played it in is somewhere inside a hotel now.

pins.title: The Front
pins.tease: For years, Phish played this address more than any room on earth
pins.stand_at: Stand on the south sidewalk of Main Street in front of the Skirack storefront at 85 Main Street, near the corner of Main and Pine.
pins.script:
You are outside 85 Main Street, at the corner of Main and Pine. Today it sells bicycles and skis.

Between May 27, 1988 and May 12, 1991, this address was a nightclub called The Front. Phish played there 54 times.

Fifty four shows. In three years. In one room.

For years that was more than any other room on earth. Not a theater. Not an arena. Not a festival field. This block. Madison Square Garden has since gone past it, and it took the Garden almost forty years.

One room on this block accounts for something like one show in forty the band has ever played.

Look at what 1988 alone looked like here. May 27. A night in June. Then July 7 and 8. Then August 11, 12 and 13, three nights running. Then September 8, 9 and 10, three more nights running. Then December 11, 12 and 15. That is a band living in a room.

And here is the thing about that. By the time it ended they were touring out of state, and they kept coming back to a nightclub on lower Main Street to play three nights in a row.

The last of the 54 was May 12, 1991.

Now the store. Skirack opened in 1969, a few blocks from where you are standing, started by twin brothers, Zandy and John Wheeler, along with a group of University of Vermont ski enthusiasts. For years they ran two separate shops on lower Main Street, one for the self-propelled sports, bikes and cross country skis and snowshoes, and one called The Downhill Edge for skiing and snowboarding. Those two eventually folded into a single storefront. In 2011 they opened a second store nearby with Patagonia.

So this address has been a bike shop longer than it was ever a nightclub.

Fifty four nights, and nothing here to tell you.

pins.title: Main Street Landing
pins.tease: Two women got this land after a hundred million dollar plan died
pins.stand_at: Stand at the corner of College and Lake streets, outside the brick and stone building whose four sides do not match.
pins.script:
Stand at this corner and walk your eyes around the building. Each face of it is different. Different materials, different rhythm, as though four separate buildings had grown together.

That was the instruction. The owners say they told their architect they wanted every facade to look like a different building, built out of local brick and stone, feeling like the pioneer shops of the eighteen hundreds. He came back with the drawing in two weeks.

Now the part that is hard to believe. In the mid nineteen eighties this corner was inside a twenty-seven acre, hundred million dollar development called the Alden Waterfront Project. Hundreds of condominiums. Offices. A seven story hotel. A large parking garage. An art museum. An ice rink. Bernie Sanders, mayor at the time, backed it. The city council backed it. In December of 1985 the bond vote that would have paid for the public pieces failed, and the whole thing collapsed.

Two women were left standing in the wreckage. Melinda Moulton had been the project's director of operations. Lisa Steele ended up owning the waterfront land. Steele phoned Moulton to help her sell it off. Moulton proposed they build it themselves instead. That company is Main Street Landing.

Here is the number that tells the story. Under the Alden plan, eleven acres had been optioned from the railroad at five hundred thousand dollars an acre. After the plan died, the city sued the railroad under the public trust doctrine, and Moulton says the land came in at sixty-five thousand dollars an acre.

Their first two buildings opened in 1995. This one, the Lake and College building, opened on July 3, 2005. A hundred and twenty thousand square feet, with a two hundred and twenty seat performing arts center inside it, and Silver LEED certification.

In February of that year it had no tenants at all. Moulton tells it this way. The anchor signed after touring an unfinished top floor at ten below zero, with plastic sheeting flapping over the window openings. That tenant was Seventh Generation, and it took thirty-six thousand square feet.

pins.title: The Falls
pins.tease: Everything Winooski became started with the water under this bridge
pins.stand_at: Stand on the west sidewalk of the Main Street bridge over the Winooski River, on the Winooski side, and look downstream toward the dam.
pins.script:
You are standing over the reason this city exists.

Below you the Winooski River drops through a rock gorge. Downstream sits a low dam with a powerhouse beside it. Everything built around you was built to use that drop.

The first person to work it was Ira Allen. In 1786 he put a dam across the river at the upper falls, with a sawmill at each end, cutting lumber for the Quebec and British markets. A village grew up around those mills. It was called Winooski Falls, and it belonged to the town of Colchester.

After Allen came the wool men. In 1835 a group of Burlington businessmen secured title to every water privilege on this bank of the river. Two years later they built a woolen mill of local stone below the lower falls, and a power canal running under it. They dammed the lower falls with timber the same year.

The river took it all back. In November 1927 a flood tore down the valley and destroyed both dams. The lower one was never repaired.

The dam you are looking at now sits at the lower falls, below Allen's site, and it is much newer. Its spillway abuts a timber crib dam built in 1876, and that older dam is still standing. The station behind it started generating on the first of April, 1993. Three turbines. About 30 million kilowatt hours in an average year. Beside it is a fish lift, run in the spring and again in the fall so fish can get past the wall.

In 2014 the City of Burlington bought the whole plant for $16 million. At the time of that sale, the plant could cover about 8 percent of Burlington's power, which works out to roughly 5,200 homes. The drop it works with, from the pond above to the river below, is about 32 feet.

One more thing about that powerhouse. It is built to be flooded and to keep working. The engineers designed it for another 1927. Water at that level would come nearly to the top of the bridge you are standing on.

pins.title: The Champlain Mill
pins.tease: Count the glass in one window and you reach forty-two panes
pins.stand_at: Stand on the walkway off Winooski Falls Way, north of the Champlain Mill, facing the long brick building.
pins.script:
Five stories of brick on a concrete foundation, standing over the river. When this went up in 1912 the company gave it a number rather than a name. The mill's own history calls it Mill Number Four.

By then the mills at these falls belonged to the American Woolen Company, which had bought the entire Burlington Woolen Company in 1902 and expanded the works into what the National Register file calls one of the most modern woolen plants in the country. This building was the newest piece of it.

On the river side the facade runs 280 feet. The end walls are 100 feet. Now look at one of the tall windows. A heavy mullion splits it down the middle, and a transom bar crosses it about a third of the way down from the top. Count the glass in a single window and you get 42 panes. There are dozens of those windows. That is what a factory looked like when daylight was the cheapest thing an owner could give a worker.

What came off the machines here was fine worsted wool. Uniform cloth for the military, for police, for railroads. Men's suiting. Fashion fabric. By 1911 electricity from the plant behind the first mill had already replaced two water-powered turbines and a backup coal furnace at the older works. During the Second World War the machines ran 24 hours a day, and about 300 people came and went at each of the three shift changes.

In 1954 American Woolen shut the Winooski mills. Defense orders had fallen off, synthetics were arriving, foreign cloth was cheaper, and running a mill in the north cost too much.

The building was taken in 1972 under the federal urban renewal program. In 1980 the inside was rebuilt for offices, shops and restaurants. In 2011 a software company bought it and restored it with $390,000 in state and federal historic tax credits, bringing more than 200 jobs into the brick. A restaurant opened here in December 2014.

Look at the northeast corner. There is a rectangular tower one story taller than the rest, and it holds every scrap of decoration this building has. None of it was applied. It is all made by corbelling, courses of brick stepped out from the wall.

pins.title: The Winooski Block
pins.tease: A wooden eagle five feet tall watched urban renewal take everything else
pins.stand_at: Stand on the sidewalk at the corner of Main Street and East Allen Street, outside the corner of the block, and look northeast at the East Allen Street front with the eagle on its cornice.
pins.script:
Look up at the brick building on the corner. High on the cornice, in wooden letters, it reads Winooski 1867 Block. Above the date is an eagle carved from a single piece of wood, with a body over five feet tall.

Ira Allen built a house on this spot around 1785, with a garden the local histories describe as a paradise of fruits and flowers.

The block went up in the year those letters claim, in the boom that came out of the Civil War. A Burlington architect named Warren Thayer designed it. Three merchants paid for it and put their businesses on the ground floor. Two local builders, Frank Peppin and Peter Villemere, raised it. The brick was made at Francis Le Clair's brickyard on Malletts Bay Avenue. The fifty pairs of cast iron window caps and sills came from the Edwards and Stevens foundry on East Canal Street, and they were the single most expensive item in the whole construction.

Behind those storefronts, the west end of the third floor was one room, 60 feet by 53. A concert hall. Through the 1870s the town's French-speaking and English-speaking Catholic parishes both used it, and so did Sherman's Cornet Band.

None of this was built by shopkeepers, though. It was built on the mills below. Down on West Canal Street the mill yard still stands: the Colchester Merino Mill, finished in 1880, extended in 1902 by a wing 150 feet long thrown right over the water race, and the Winooski Worsted Mill of 1895 beside it. There is a brick boarding house from about 1840 that was originally six row houses for mill workers. The mill buildings hold apartments now. The loft conversion started in 1979 and the first resident moved in during 1981.

Here is what makes this corner strange. In 1973 most of Winooski's commercial architecture was demolished to comply with an urban renewal plan. This block survived. Everything between it and the river came down, and for thirty years it stood almost alone on a rise of open land, in a direct visual line from the Burlington bridge.
