pins.title: The Circle
pins.tease: This city once seriously planned to seal itself under a dome
pins.stand_at: Cross at one of the marked crosswalks into Victory Circle, the landscaped island in the middle of the Winooski roundabout, and stand on the paths inside. Stay on the path and don't walk in the traffic lanes.
pins.script:
You are standing on an island in the middle of a traffic circle, with Main Street running around you in both directions.

Apart from the brick block just to the north, almost nothing you can see is old, and that is not an accident. In 1973 most of Winooski's commercial architecture was demolished to comply with an urban renewal plan. Two downtown blocks came down for parking. The city then spent decades with a hole in its middle.

Which brings us to 1979, and the strangest chapter this city has. Mark Tigan was Winooski's director of community development, and he was fighting a plan by Burlington to build a dam at the upper falls, a dam that would have taken away Winooski's biggest asset. An energy lawyer told him to file a competing application for a smaller dam of his own, just to get legal standing. After one city council meeting, Tigan and his colleagues went out for a glass of wine and started feeling guilty about scheming to generate more power when they had spent no time on saving any. So they started brainstorming. Somebody said: put a dome over the city.

They worked out that a dome could cut residents' heating bills by up to 90 percent. The council voted 3 to 2 to apply for a $55,000 federal grant. The morning after that vote, Tigan says, about ten satellite trucks were parked outside City Hall. Residents formed the Golden Onion Dome Club. A local restaurant sold a dessert called the Domessert.

Federal housing officials pulled the money once the story went international, but they sent three people from the Tennessee Valley Authority to run the study anyway: an economist, an engineer and a sociologist. The engineer said a dome over the whole city was feasible, and recommended limiting it to downtown.

The findings were presented at the first and only International Dome Symposium, held at Saint Michael's College on the 26th and 27th of March, 1980. Buckminster Fuller, who invented the geodesic dome and was 85 years old, flew in from Brazil to give the keynote.

pins.title: Onion City
pins.tease: They built the school first and let the church wait
pins.stand_at: Stand on the West Allen Street sidewalk in front of Winooski City Hall at 27 West Allen Street, with the building in front of you.
pins.script:
This is Winooski City Hall, 27 West Allen Street. The city it runs is about a square mile and a half. At the 2020 census, 7,997 people lived inside it.

The mills brought most of the families who first filled it. Hundreds of them came down from Quebec to work the looms, French-speaking and Catholic, and they arrived faster than any institution could keep up.

In 1862 the Bishop of Burlington, Louis De Goesbriand, asked the Sisters of Providence to take on the children of Winooski. At first the sisters walked over from a Catholic orphanage in Burlington every day. In 1863 they rented rooms in the Baxter Block, in the middle of the village, and taught two classes, one for the boys and one for the girls.

In 1868 a priest named Jean Audet arrived from Quebec to lead the parish. He could have built a church first. He built a school. Saint Louis Convent and School were blessed by the bishop in January 1869. A hundred and forty children enrolled. Families paid fifty cents a month for each child. If you had three or more, the third cost twenty-five cents, and the rest were free.

The church came later. In the meantime the parish rented halls. Through the 1870s the French-speaking and English-speaking Catholic parishes shared the third-floor concert hall of the Winooski Block, a few hundred feet up the hill from here, and shared it with the local cornet band.

That pattern of arrival never stopped. Winooski is a designated refugee resettlement community, and the regional planning commission describes it as the most diverse community in the state, with over 30 languages spoken by residents.

The name of this place comes from the oldest arrivals of all. The Abenaki named the river for the wild onions growing along its banks. Ira Allen first dammed the falls down the hill from here. He and his brothers called their land company the Onion River Company.

pins.title: The First Ben & Jerry's
pins.tease: An ice cream empire started in a gas station right here
pins.stand_at: Stand on the southwest corner of College and St. Paul streets and look down at the sidewalk for a bronze plaque.
pins.script:
Look down at the sidewalk. Somewhere near your feet on this corner there is a bronze plaque set into the sidewalk. It marks a gas station that is no longer here.

On May 5, 1978, two friends opened an ice cream shop in a renovated gas station on this corner, College and St. Paul. They had taken a correspondence course in ice cream making from the creamery at Pennsylvania State University. They had about twelve thousand dollars. Their names were Ben Cohen and Jerry Greenfield.

That is the whole origin of Ben and Jerry's. Not a factory. Not Waterbury. A repurposed filling station at a downtown intersection, opening in May, in a state where the ice cream season is short and the first winter is the real test.

They got through the winter. And in those early years they did something with the building that would be hard to arrange now. They projected movies onto the big wall beside the shop, and people stood around outside with cones and watched.

At their celebrations out front they staged a bit. Jerry would announce a rare visit from a mystic from the east. Then Ben would appear, barefoot, wrapped in white sheets, wearing a turban, to the sound of Rubberband Man by the Spinners. He would lie down and bare his stomach. Jerry would balance a cinder block on it and bring down a sledgehammer.

The shop is gone. The building was torn down. What is here now is a surface parking lot, which is about the least romantic possible ending for the birthplace of Ben and Jerry's.

The plaque came in 1988, for the company's tenth anniversary. They pressed it into the sidewalk at this corner and printed up T-shirts that read: BE 10 AGAIN.

It is the only thing left on the site.

pins.title: The Mall Block
pins.tease: Burlington tore down a mall and then stared at the hole
pins.stand_at: Stand on Church Street at the Cherry Street corner and look west, into the block behind the storefronts.
pins.script:
Look west into this block. Within living memory it has been an enclosed shopping mall, an open hole in the ground, and a construction site.

The mall came first. It opened on November 1, 1976 as the Burlington Square Mall. Its anchor was a department store called Porteous. An indoor mall, dropped into the middle of a downtown that already had a pedestrian shopping street. Later it was renamed the Burlington Town Center. Filene's, later Macy's, arrived in 1999. L.L. Bean came in 2014.

In December of 2013 an investor group bought the property for twenty-five million dollars, and in November of 2014 announced a two hundred million dollar plan to knock it down and build something much bigger. Demolition began in December 2017. Then the work stopped.

For four years the middle of downtown Burlington was an open excavation. People called it the pit. Not affectionately. The last businesses in the surviving stub of the mall shut for good in early 2022.

Construction restarted in 2022, under local developers. In September of 2025 the first building opened: a hundred and sixty-one room hotel, fifty-three apartments, ground floor retail, a restaurant and a cafe. Studios listed between sixteen hundred fifty and nineteen hundred fifty dollars a month. The two bedroom on the top floor listed at sixty eight hundred.

And the project got a new name, which is the part worth noticing. Burlington Square Mall became Burlington Town Center, became CityPlace Burlington, and is now called Burlington Square. After fifty years and one very long hole, the block is back to almost exactly the name it started with.

The second building, roughly three hundred and twenty more apartments and another hotel, is still going up. Seventy-three of the units are meant to be affordable. In May of 2026 the city council voted unanimously to push the deadline for those units to the end of 2027. As of August 2026 none of them had been built, and the second building is aimed at late 2027.

pins.title: The Boathouse
pins.tease: The building you are looking at is floating
pins.stand_at: Stand at the foot of College Street on the landward approach, where the pavement meets the boathouse.
pins.script:
The boathouse in front of you is floating.

It does not rest on pilings and it is not built on fill. It is moored to them by steel rings, and it rises and falls with the lake. In May of 1988 crews floated a barge into place at the base of College Street and built the boathouse on top of it. It was seven years old, bought down in Texas for forty one thousand dollars. Work started on May 21. It opened to the public shortly before the Fourth of July that same summer.

That is fast, and it was the point. Burlington was trying to turn an industrial shoreline into a public one, and the boathouse was, as one account puts it, the cornerstone of the city's lakefront revival. The bike path along the water had opened two years before.

The design imitates something that used to stand on this exact water.

The Lake Champlain Yacht Club was founded on this working waterfront in 1887. There was no land to be had, so in 1888 the club built its first two-story clubhouse out over the water, on pilings.

It burned in 1901.

They built another one. That one burned in 1911.

They built a third. In 1936 the club sold it to the Green Mountain Adirondack Ferry Company, which turned it into a ferry station. The club's own history says it had been declared unsafe and too expensive to fix. The club went inactive during the war years, then came back. They bought into Shelburne again in 1962 and put up a modest new clubhouse there in 1963.

Then the city went looking for a design for a public boathouse. The architect who won it, Marcel Beaudin, was a yacht club member. He drew the new building to echo the old clubhouses. As the club tells it, his pitch included a photograph of the 1888 clubhouse so officials could see the link.

The barge you are looking at floats on the spot where those pilings stood.

pins.title: The Firehouse
pins.tease: That tower was built to hang wet hoses in
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Church Street Marketplace bricks directly in front of 135 Church Street, looking up at the brick tower.
pins.script:
Look up. The brick tower above you is 85 feet tall, and it was not built for the bell.

It was built to hang fire hoses in, so they could dry. That is the whole reason it is that shape: a narrow shaft tall enough to hold a length of wet hose hanging straight down.

This is the Ethan Allen Firehouse, 135 Church Street, designed by the local architect A. B. Fisher and built in 1887. The style is a commercial variation of Richardsonian Romanesque.

It was home to the Ethan Allen Engine Company Number Four, one of the city's volunteer fire companies. And a volunteer engine house was more than an emergency service. It was where the members socialized, broke bread, and shared ideas. A private club that also happened to put out your fire.

The company started with horse-drawn equipment. Later it was folded into the city's fire department, and the building was adapted to house motorized fire equipment. After that the Burlington Police Department moved in, and stayed until the late 1960s.

It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places on April 16, 1971.

Here is the surprise. The bell that belongs in that tower spent decades somewhere else. It ended up in the collection of the Shelburne Museum, down the road, an artifact of a building still standing on Church Street.

Then it came back. In 2002 the original bell was hoisted back into the firehouse tower, where it had hung when the building was new.

Burlington City Arts had already moved a gallery into half of the ground floor in 1995. In 2002 the whole building opened to the public as the Firehouse Center for the Visual Arts. It is now the BCA Center: contemporary art exhibitions in a nineteenth-century engine house, under a tower designed to dry hose.

pins.title: The Follett House
pins.tease: The columns face the lake because the money came off the lake
pins.stand_at: Stand on the College Street sidewalk just west of the white-columned brick mansion, uphill from Battery Street, and look back at the front.
pins.script:
Six fluted Ionic columns, a pediment, and a front that does not face the street. The house is turned west, toward the lake. That was deliberate. The money that built it came off the water.

Timothy Follett was a shipping man on Lake Champlain, and at the peak of his fortune he built a house to prove it. He put it up in 1840 and hired Ammi B. Young to design it. Young is the architect of Vermont's second State House, in Montpelier. What he built here is brick, two and a half stories, on a cut stone foundation, five bays across, with a balcony running the full width of the second floor.

Then Follett changed businesses. In 1845 he became the first president of the railroad that became the Rutland and Burlington. Railroads were the future, and the future ruined him. The line failed, Follett lost his fortune in the 1850s, and he lost the house with it. He died a few years later.

The building kept going without him. A square cupola went on in the 1880s. Institutions moved through it, including at one point the local Veterans of Foreign Wars chapter. Since 1885 it has held institutional tenants rather than a family. It was listed on the National Register of Historic Places in 1972.

Then the near miss. The Pomerleau real estate agency acquired the property in 1978 to restore it, and a damaging fire hit at the very start of the project. The restoration was finished anyway. The house has been offices since.

Look down College Street toward the water and try to picture the ridge above the harbor lined with houses like this one, built by men who owned boats. This is one of the last of Burlington's grand nineteenth-century lakeside mansions.

pins.title: The Howard Opera House
pins.tease: There was a theater for well over a thousand people above these shop windows
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Church Street Marketplace bricks a few steps out from the corner of Church and Bank, and look up above the shop windows on the west corner.
pins.script:
You are standing under a theater. Look above the shop windows on this corner. Brick, a hundred and thirty feet along Church Street, seventy-six feet along Bank, sixty feet tall. Behind that wall, on the upper floors, there used to be an auditorium with enough chairs for between thirteen hundred and fourteen hundred people.

John Purple Howard paid for it. Burlington born, he went to New York as a young man and made a fortune in the hotel business. In 1877, when word got around that he was putting up a business block on this corner, townspeople started lobbying him to include a hall. The theater in City Hall was too small, they said, unsafe, and an acoustical outrage.

He agreed. He hired Stephen Hatch, another Vermonter who had gone to New York, and told him the building should be as good as anybody's. He was prepared to spend about a hundred thousand dollars.

It opened on the evening of February 24, 1879, with a touring company singing Lucia di Lammermoor. Gas fixtures lit the walls, and gas jets hidden inside the dome made heat, which pulled the air upward and ventilated the room.

Electric light arrived in October of 1886. And the manager used it only in the foyer, and in the auditorium between the acts. Touring companies wanted the gas kept burning during the show. Gaslight was warm, and it threw softer shadows on an actor's face.

On November 14, 1881, Howard gave the entire block away. Stores, theater, hall and weather station, all of it, to the Home for Destitute Children. The deed said the block could not be sold and the theater could not close before November of 1901.

The merchants downstairs eventually bought out the theater lease. Their fire insurance was brutal, because of all that flammable space over their heads.

The last performance was November 30, 1904.

pins.title: The King Street Ferry Dock
pins.tease: The dock is still here. The ferry is not.
pins.stand_at: Stand on the dock apron just west of the ferry terminal building at the foot of King Street, facing out at the open water.
pins.script:
There is a ferry terminal beside you. Look at the water. There is no ferry.

Lake Champlain Transportation says it has been carrying people across this lake since 1826. Two hundred years. The company still runs two crossings, and both of them are somewhere else. Grand Isle to Plattsburgh runs around the clock, all year, breaking ice when it has to, and takes about twelve minutes. Charlotte to Essex runs year round as well, weather permitting.

The Burlington boat went to Port Kent, New York, and it was the long one. It crossed the maximum width of Lake Champlain. It took about an hour. It never ran in winter. It was less a commute than a passage, and people used it that way.

It last operated in 2019. It has not run since.

In June of 2022 the company said the line was postponed for the near future. Staffing was tight. The pandemic had wrecked the economics. By then the loading apparatus had already been pulled off this terminal, maintenance work had been moved north to Grand Isle, and the company was talking about putting a restaurant on the site instead.

On the New York side, a town supervisor said the loss had cut into tourism and forced residents to drive to other ferry terminals. The company has not announced a return.

So this is a dock with no crossing. The building is here. The schedule is not. The water in front of you is the widest part of the lake, and on a clear day the far shore is the place the boat used to land.

The ferry company carries around a million passengers across Lake Champlain a year. Not one of them from this dock.

pins.title: The Masonic Temple
pins.tease: Vermont's Masons built a castle at the top of Church Street
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Church Street bricks just south of Pearl, out from the storefronts, and look up at the gray stone building with the steep pyramid roof.
pins.script:
Look up. Five stories of rough gray stone, and a slate roof that climbs to a pyramid over the corner. This is the Masonic Temple, at the head of Church Street, where Church meets Pearl.

It went up in 1897 and 1898. Not as a store. Not as an office block. It was built to be the state headquarters of the Grand Lodge of Vermont, Free and Accepted Masons.

The Masons had wanted this for a long time. The Grand Lodge picked Burlington as the site back in 1868. Thirty years went by before the building existed. When it was done it had cost about eighty-seven thousand dollars.

They hired John McArthur Harris, of the Philadelphia firm Wilson Brothers and Company. He gave them Richardsonian Romanesque. Heavy masonry. Round arches. A roof with real weight to it. Step around to the Pearl Street side and look at the windows there. They climb the wall at an angle. That is a staircase, showing through the stone.

The lodge rooms were upstairs. The ground floor was rented out to shops and offices from the start. A temple with storefronts under it, and rent coming in off the street.

That is not how it went. The building was expensive to keep warm. The Masons were already talking about selling it in 1914, sixteen years after they finished it, because of the heating bills. A fire in 1933 did about sixty thousand dollars of damage. Membership thinned through the rest of the century. In the mid nineteen eighties a local partnership bought the building and renovated it, lifting it onto new foundations and opening up windows that had been bricked shut.

Now every floor is retail and offices. No lodge meets here. The last Burlington lodge merged away in 2016 and moved out to Williston.

The building is protected all the same. It is one of three in the Head of Church Street Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on July 15, 1974. The other two are the brick meetinghouse above you and the turreted building across the street.

pins.title: Richardson Place
pins.tease: The turrets say Richardson but everyone here says Abernethy's
pins.stand_at: Stand on the west side of the Church Street mall, a little below Pearl, looking back up the hill at the brick building with the round turrets.
pins.script:
Up the hill from you, on the east side of Church Street, there is a castle. Brick, with round bays that bulge out from the corners and finish in cone-shaped roofs, and dormers punched into a steep roofline.

The style is called Chateauesque. Chateau, French for castle. It is one of very few buildings in Burlington that use it.

This is 2 Church Street, built in 1895, and it did not go up as a shop. It went up as a department store, the largest in Burlington, planted at the top of the hill where Church Street starts.

That siting was not an accident of the market. Church Street runs four blocks, from Pearl at the top down to Main at the bottom. From almost anywhere on it, if you look uphill, the white church closes the view, and this building is one of the two that frame it.

It is one of three buildings in the Head of Church Street Historic District, all added to the National Register of Historic Places together in July of 1974. A church, a Masonic lodge and a store, at one intersection.

Now look at the small balconies on the front. There is a letter worked into the ironwork. An R. That is the Richardson in Richardson Place, from the year it opened. Abernethy's covered those R's with gold A's, and the R's came back in nineteen eighty-three.

Here is the thing. Almost nobody who grew up in Burlington calls this the Richardson Building. They call it Abernethy's. Abernethy's Department Store filled these floors for decades, selling high-end clothing and accessories for men and women, and it stayed until the 1980s. The store was here so long that the name stuck to the building and never came off.

The R is back on the railing. The name people actually use belongs to somebody else.

pins.title: St. Paul's Cathedral
pins.tease: The church burned and the city traded it a lake view
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Cherry Street side of the concrete cathedral, out past its west wall on the lake side, facing the water.
pins.script:
In front of you is a wall of raw concrete. Poured in place, left rough, nothing faced over it. This is the Cathedral Church of St. Paul, and that tall element beside the sanctuary is a bell tower.

Go closer to it. The bells inside are older than everything around them. There are eight of them, cast in 1895 by the Meneely bell foundry in Troy, New York. They spent their first seventy-six years hanging in a completely different building.

That building was a Gothic Revival stone church, dedicated in 1832, and it stood on Bank Street between St. Paul and Pine, a few blocks east of here and up the hill. The parish had organized in 1830. Its first service was held in the old courthouse on June 12, 1831. The church was enlarged three times, in 1851, in 1866, and in 1910. In 1965 the diocese made it the cathedral of Vermont.

On a February night in 1971, it burned.

What happened next only happens in a city in the middle of urban renewal. The parish's block, occupied for almost a hundred and forty years, was useful to the city's redevelopment plans. So the city offered a trade. Land down here, on the edge of the bluff, looking west at Lake Champlain and the Adirondacks.

They took it. An international design competition went to Thomas Cullins and William Henderson of Burlington Associates. The new cathedral was consecrated on November 11, 1973, less than three years after the fire.

Inside it is concrete, white oak, acoustic panelling and slate, with a glass wall aimed at the water. Outside it is Brutalism, and the concrete is doing exactly what the style asks for: it shows you how the building was made.

The building is 1973. The bells in its tower were cast in 1895.

pins.title: The Flynn
pins.tease: Vermont opened a half-million-dollar palace into the Depression
pins.stand_at: Stand on the Main Street sidewalk outside 153 Main Street, facing the marquee.
pins.script:
You are looking at the marquee of the Flynn, 153 Main Street. Flat facade, big lit sign, the whole thing pushed right up to the sidewalk.

On the night of Wednesday, November 26, 1930, floodlights danced above Burlington to herald what was billed as Vermont's newest and largest entertainment palace. It cost 500,000 dollars. It was the idea of a local entrepreneur named John J. Flynn and his investors in the Queen City Realty Company, and it was designed as a state-of-the-art facility for both touring stars of vaudeville and motion pictures.

Sit with that date for a second. November 1930. The stock market had crashed thirteen months earlier. Burlington opened a half-million-dollar Art Deco theater into the first full winter of the Great Depression.

Here is the surprise. The building was designed for live vaudeville, and the first thing that ever ran on that stage was a movie. A comedy called Big Money.

The architects were William Luther Mowll and Roger Glade Rand. What they delivered was not just a hall. Flynn and his backers called it an entertainment complex, a state-of-the-art facility built to hold two kinds of show at once.

There was an organ, too. A Wurlitzer built in 1925, opus 1200, Style H. It started life at Burlington's Majestic Theatre, moved here, and by most accounts ended up in a Burlington convent.

Then multiplexes arrived in the 1970s and the theater declined. Lyric Theatre had been staging shows here since nineteen seventy-four, and in nineteen eighty-one restoration of the Art Deco theater began. A second wave of work in the late 1990s and early 2000s took the interior back toward its original look and added FlynnSpace, a smaller performance venue downstairs.

It stopped being a movie house. It runs on live performance now, as the Flynn Center for the Performing Arts.

The Flynn was recognized by the Art Deco Societies of America as one of the country's ten most important Art Deco restoration projects.
